findings.title: Uncovering a New Device Code Phishing Campaign
findings.summary_md: Independent researcher Paul Newton documented a phishing campaign abusing Microsoft device code authentication through Cloudflare workers.dev domains whose subdomains embed the victim's email address, with a '/api/device/start' + X-Antibot-Token page flow that auto-copies the code and redirects to adobe.com after token capture. The post published KQL hunting queries, including 'SigninLogs | where AuthenticationProtocol == "deviceCode"' and a first-time device code auth hunt (hunt-2025-043) with a 30-day lookback filtered to ResultType == 0, plus sender domains registered between 1995 and 2017.

findings.title: Device Code-based OAuth Phishing
findings.summary_md: Unit 42's timely threat intel note, dated March 23, 2026, tracked an active device code phishing campaign impersonating a cloud file storage service and two e-signature platforms, with its earliest observation on Feb 18, 2026. It detailed AES-GCM encrypted payloads delivered via Cloudflare Workers, cookie exfiltration, anti-analysis tricks such as debugger traps and DevTools detection, and listed workers.dev indicators overlapping Sekoia's EvilTokens set, including index-ap3.tyler2miler-proton-me-s-account.workers.dev.

findings.title: New widespread EvilTokens kit: device code phishing as-a-service - Part 1
findings.summary_md: Sekoia's TDR team published the first public technical analysis of the EvilTokens kit on March 30, 2026, after privately distributing it as FLINT report 2025-038 on March 25, having first identified the service in phishing-focused criminal communities on March 3, 2026, with pages circulating since mid-February. The analysis documents the backend REST API (api/device/start, api/prt/convert, api/prt/cookie generating the x-ms-RefreshTokenCredential cookie for browser SSO hijack), rolling 90-day refresh tokens and Primary Refresh Token conversion, 66 phishing attachments collected by March 19, over 1,000 urlscan hits by March 23, the distinctive X-Antibot-Token header, Cloudflare Workers domain naming patterns, and a YARA rule (creation date 2026-03-05).

findings.title: EvilTokens: an AI-augmented Phishing-as-a-Service for automating BEC fraud - Part 2
findings.summary_md: Part 2, published April 7, 2026, details the Telegram-based operation run by eviltokensadmin since Feb 17, 2026: the $1,500 Office 365 capture link with lifetime panel access plus a $500 monthly licence, a ~280-subscriber private group as of March 19, and NOWPayments crypto billing. It maps the AI fraud pipeline: Graph API reconnaissance of inbox rules, contacts, calendars and sent items, ingestion of up to 5,000 stolen emails in batches of 250 through the Groq API using llama-3.1-8b-instant, BEC scenario drafting with llama-3.3-70b-versatile, gpt-4o-mini for translation, and a $500 Portal Browser for operating stolen sessions.

findings.title: How EvilTokens Turbocharges Old School Phishing with AI
findings.summary_md: Huntress's May 11, 2026 writeup reconstructs the campaign telemetry behind its earlier 344-organization, five-country, 16-day wave: first alerts on Feb 19 and Feb 24, escalation on March 2, one cloud IP hitting 50 organizations in a single week, and relaying through the Railway.com PaaS. It notes the lures passed Cisco Secure Email, Trend Micro and Mimecast untouched, and that Huntress pushed a conditional access policy blocking Railway infrastructure across more than 60,000 tenants.

findings.title: What is EvilTokens?: The PhaaS Platform That Tells Attackers What to Do After They Get In
findings.summary_md: Flare's Emerging Threats researcher Assaf Morag profiled EvilTokens on Aug 24, 2026, one day before the takedown coverage cycle, tying together the $1,500 plus $500-per-month pricing, the 16-day 344-organization wave, and Sekoia's infrastructure findings of 66 lure attachments and 1,000+ related infrastructure results. The post frames the platform's significance as the commoditization of post-compromise work: inbox analysis, stakeholder mapping and AI-generated fraud messages sold as features rather than skills.
